Early life stages of Chinook salmon (Oncorhynchus tshawytscha) are characterized by substantial maternal investment, with each fertilized egg containing an initial energy content of 2775 joules . This energetic endowment supports the embryo through a prolonged incubation period; emerging alevins typically hatch after 121 days [ab = 121 days] when reared at a stable temperature of 8 °C [T = 8 °C]. Upon hatching, the newly emerged larvae possess a modest fork length of 3.47 centimeters [Lb = 3.47 centimeters] and a corresponding wet weight of 0.515 grams [Wwb = 0.515 grams], reflecting the average condition observed in hatchery-reared Chinook populations. The yolk-sac stage involves progressive absorption of endogenous nutrients, with the dry weight of the egg itself having been recorded at approximately 0.128 grams , a product of the typical yolk composition of this species.

As juvenile Chinook salmon transition to exogenous feeding and initiate their downstream migration, growth trajectories become increasingly influenced by ambient thermal regimes. Under conditions typical of productive riverine habitats at 13 °C [T = 13 °C], these fish exhibit a remarkably compressed life cycle, with the maximum documented lifespan reaching 1460 days [am = 1460 days] before the semelparous adults succumb following spawning. This relatively short lifespan is coupled with an early onset of reproductive maturation; first reproduction occurs at 1095 days after hatching [tR = 1095 days after hatching], a timing that aligns closely with the three-year return migration observed in many coastal Chinook runs at a temperature of 13 °C [T = 13 °C]. The species' ultimate body size, attained by the largest individuals in oceanic feeding grounds, reaches a fork length of 150 centimeters [Li = 150 centimeters], with the corresponding ultimate wet weight of those same large adults documented at 65000 grams [Wwi = 65000 grams], a value typical of particularly robust male Chinook.

Morphometric relationships in Chinook salmon provide important tools for assessing population structure and individual condition at key life history transitions. At the onset of sexual maturity, individuals typically achieve a fork length of 68 centimeters [Lp = 68 centimeters], which serves as a reliable predictor of reproductive readiness. The wet weight of these pubertal fish, estimated from established length-weight regressions for mature adults and incorporating gonad mass, is approximately 4786.41 grams [Wwp = approximately 4786.41 grams], a value that reflects the substantial somatic and reproductive investment required before first spawning. By contrast, the wet weight of males that have attained their ultimate size is considerably greater, reaching approximately 4786.41 grams , indicating that while length increases considerably after puberty, mass gain is disproportionately allocated toward reproductive structures in the final year of life.

Spawning females exhibit a clear relationship between body size and reproductive output, a pattern well-documented across Pacific salmonids. At a postorbital-hypural length of 73 centimeters , typically observed in four-year-old spawning individuals, fecundity reaches 5820 eggs  when measured at a water temperature of 13 °C [T = 13 °C]. This substantial clutch size underscores the high reproductive effort characteristic of semelparous salmon, where a single spawning event represents the entirety of lifetime reproductive investment. The energetic cost of producing such a large number of relatively yolky eggs is considerable; the initial energy content of each ovum, at 2775 joules , combined with the dry weight of each egg at 0.128 grams , illustrates the magnitude of maternal provisioning required to sustain embryonic development through the lengthy incubation period.

Comparative analyses across Pacific salmon species reveal that Chinook salmon exhibit some of the largest body sizes and highest fecundities in the genus Oncorhynchus. The ultimate fork length of 150 centimeters [Li = 150 centimeters] and ultimate wet weight of 65000 grams [Wwi = 65000 grams] place this species among the most massive of the anadromous salmonids, surpassed only by certain populations of the closely related Oncorhynchus masou. This large body size is reflected in the substantial investment per offspring; the wet weight at birth of 0.515 grams [Wwb = 0.515 grams] is notably greater than that observed in congeners such as pink or chum salmon. The remarkable life-history strategy of Chinook salmon, combining a maximum lifespan of 1460 days [am = 1460 days] with a single, catastrophic reproductive event at approximately 1095 days after hatching [tR = approximately 1095 days after hatching], exemplifies the evolutionary trade-offs inherent in semelparous migration, where rapid growth and high fecundity are balanced against the absolute certainty of post-spaw at a temperature of 13 °C [T = 13 °C] at a temperature of 13 °C [T = 13 °C]ning mortality.
